 JAKARTA, KOMPAS.com - The National Disaster Mitigation Agency (BNPB) has urged local governments to continue mapping disaster-prone areas during the rainy season down to the village level.
 "The most important thing is that national and provincial mapping should be followed up by district/city governments with more detailed mapping down to the village level," said Acting Head of the Data, Information, and Communication Center for Disaster Management at BNPB, Berton SP Panjaitan, in a statement on Tuesday (3/11/2026).
 The Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) predicts the peak of the rainy season will occur starting December 2026. 
 As the intensity of rainfall increases, several regions are beginning to experience high rainfall levels.
 According to BMKG data as of November 3, 2026, this condition has been observed in parts of Aceh, North Sumatra, West Sumatra, South Sumatra, West Kalimantan, Central Sulawesi, and Papua.
 However, high rainfall is not the only factor determining the occurrence of hydrometeorological disasters.
 Topographical conditions, soil characteristics, watershed areas, sedimentation, and drainage capacity also influence the vulnerability of a region.
 Andri Ramdhani, Acting Deputy for Meteorology at BMKG, stated that these factors create varying potential for flooding and landslides across different areas.
 "Disasters are also influenced by topographical conditions, soil characteristics, watershed areas, sedimentation, drainage capacity, and the local environmental conditions of each region," Andri told Kompas.com on Tuesday (3/11/2026).
 Here are the regions that have been mapped for disaster vulnerability during the rainy season.
 From Aceh to NTT
 Acting Head of the Data, Information, and Communication Center for Disaster Management at BNPB, Berton Panjaitan, identified several regions categorized as disaster-prone during this rainy season.
 Berton explained that this data was obtained after BNPB conducted mapping of disaster-prone areas through risk assessment studies and the InaRISK portal.
 "This mapping includes potential flooding, landslides, flash floods, and other threats," Berton stated on Tuesday.
 Mapping Needs to Continue by Local Governments
 However, Berton reminded that the level of vulnerability varies by type of disaster for each region. Therefore, he requested that national mapping be promptly continued by district/city governments down to the village level.
 "The most important thing is that national and provincial mapping should be followed up by district/city governments with more detailed mapping down to the village level," he emphasized.
